sec.title: Background
sec.p: Hemodynamic instability, a life-threatening condition marked by circulatory failure, presents a significant challenge in intensive care unit (ICU) settings, often leading to poor patient outcomes. Traditional monitoring methods that rely on single parameters may delay diagnosis. Machine learning models offer a solution by integrating multiple clinical parameters to more dynamically and accurately predict instability.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We developed the Time-varying Hemodynamic Early Warning Score (TvHEWS), an AI-assisted model used to predict hemodynamic instability in intensive care unit (ICU) patients. The model was trained and internally validated via retrospective data from the VGHTPE 2010 cohort (2010–2021) at Taipei Veteran General Hospital. It was further validated with prospective data from the VGHTPE 2022 cohort and external data from the MIMIC IV cohort. TvHEWS includes hourly updating models, providing continuous risk assessments.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: TvHEWS showed strong predictive performance. In the VGHTPE 2010 cohort, the AUROC was 0.93, with a precision of 0.94 and a recall of 0.77. In the VGHTPE 2022 cohort, the AUROC was 0.92, with precision and recall balanced at 0.74 and 0.76, respectively. The MIMIC IV cohort had a slightly lower AUROC of 0.82, with a precision of 0.72 and a recall of 0.36. The calibration plots showed good alignment between the predicted and observed risks, with Brier scores of 0.082, 0.085, and 0.116 for the VGHTPE 2010, VGHTPE 2022, and MIMIC IV cohorts, respectively. TvHEWS predicted hemodynamic instability for up to 7 h before intervention in the VGHTPE 2010 cohort, 8.6 h in the VGHTPE 2022 cohort, and 21 h in the MIMIC IV cohort, with low false alarm rates.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: TvHEWS addresses the challenge of early detection of hemodynamic instability by integrating multiple clinical parameters and offering continuous, dynamic risk assessments. It enhances the ability to anticipate and manage critical circulatory issues, potentially improving patient outcomes through earlier interventions. Further prospective validation in other hospitals is needed to confirm its robustness across diverse settings.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Hemodynamic instability, characterized by life-threatening circulatory failure and insufficient cellular oxygen utilization, affects more than one-third of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, with associated mortality ranging from 40–59% [1]. Hypotension is one of the typical symptoms of critical patients with hemodynamic instability, but it may lead to a delayed diagnosis if only single parameters such as blood pressure or calculations based on single parameters, such as the shock index, are monitored [2]. Multiple clinical parameters reflecting cardiovascular system physiology, tissue perfusion, and cellular metabolism over time [3] are essential for predicting hemodynamic instability and facilitating early decision-making and interventions.

A data-rich ICU environment amplifies the challenge of identifying crucial information from large quantities of alarm on multiple clinical parameters due to alarm fatigue and human cognitive limitations [4]. Machine learning (ML) techniques have already demonstrated potential benefits in the detection and classification of diseases with multiple parameters and outperform traditional early warning scores in the ICU [5]. Multiparameter ML models are empowered to detect high-risk hemodynamic instability, incorporating vital signs, laboratory data, blood gas measurements, and ventilation settings, predominantly [6–8]. Traditionally, a single, static model estimating risk at a specific time window, cannot be robust to the impact caused by transient outliers and incapable of reflecting the evolving clinical condition of ICU patients.

In this study, we developed a dynamic early warning system with 24 time-varying machine learning models named the Time-varying Hemodynamic Early Warning Score (TvHEWS), allowing clinicians to assess hemodynamic risk continuously over a 24-hour period. The performance of the TvHEWS was further validated in prospective and external cohorts to ensure robustness. Additionally, we introduced an alpha value to adjust for cohort variations, demonstrating its potential applicability in clinical settings. This architecture allows for a more resilient and physiologically relevant representation of patient trajectories. Nevertheless, generalizability remains a challenge when deploying such systems in external populations with heterogeneous clinical practices, due to disparities in data collection methods, EMR infrastructures, equipment, and patient characteristics [9].

sec.title: Participants, data sources, study design, and setting
sec.p: This study was conducted in the mixed ICU of Taipei Veteran General Hospital (VGHTPE). We trained the model based on data from patients over 20 years of age admitted between January 1, 2010, and December 31, 2021, i.e. VGHTPE2010 cohort. Data from ICU admission to discharge were extracted from the Philips IntelliSpace Critical Care and Anesthesia (ICCA) system. Patients with incomplete data or ICU stays shorter than 6 h were excluded, as detailed in the study flow diagram (Fig. 1). Ethical approval was obtained from VGHTPE’s ethical committee (No. 2020-09-001AC) and the Philips Internal Committee of Biomedical Experiments (ICBE-S-00737). Data from January to June 2022 at the same hospital, i.e. VGHTPE 2022 cohort, was utilized for internal prospective cohort. The Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC IV) cohort, consisting of patient admissions from 2008 to 2019 at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) [10]served as an external validation dataset. Both the VGHTPE 2022 and the MIMIC IV cohort followed the same inclusion and exclusion criteria as the VGHTPE 2010 cohort. Importantly, there was no overlap in the data between the VGHTPE 2010 cohort and the VGHTPE 2022 cohort.

sec.title: Hemodynamic instability annotation
sec.p: We defined hemodynamic instability in patients by annotating segments where interventions such as the administration of vasoactive/inotropic drugs, fluid therapy, and packed red cells occurred (eTable 1). A patient experiencing hemodynamic instability could have multiple such segments during their ICU stay; however, for this study, only the first segment occurring after 6 h in the ICU was considered. Segments within the first 6 h were excluded to focus on subsequent interventions, ensuring a consistent baseline for assessing the onset of instability and its management (eFig. 1). This approach was applied consistently across the training, internal validation, and external validation phases. Annotation rules were defined by clinicians in VGHTPE and conducted by independent personnel.

sec.title: Data processing and variable selection
sec.p: Initially, we assessed 63 variables from the literature for the early detection of hemodynamic instability and circulatory shock (eTable 2). The selection process excluded variables with high missing ratios (> 60%), significant correlations (Pearson’s ratio ≥ 0.8, p < 0.05), and nonsignificant outcomes in stepwise logistic regression (p > 0.05). After discussing with clinical experts, we re-included certain variables that were initially excluded during multivariable feature selection but demonstrated good clinical relevance and moderate predictive power (AUROC > 0.50) in univariable decision tree analysis, resulting in final 46 key predictors remaining for the study. Plausibility checks were then conducted to ensure physiological validity, with outliers replaced by null values, as detailed in eTable 3. For patients in the unstable group, time-varying data for each variable were extracted hourly, leading to the onset of hemodynamic interventions, whereas for the stable group, data were collected within a 6-hour observation window post-ICU admission. Missing values were handled via a nonrandom missingness strategy. The latest available measurements during a certain forward time windows were used for hourly values, e.g., 2 h for heart rate, and 26 h for laboratory tests, as shown in eTable 3. Noninvasive blood pressure readings were substituted for unavailable invasive measurements, and the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) was set to a standard room level of 21% if not specified. Detailed features’ distribution of training cohort VGHTPE 2010 is shown in eTable 4. For external validation, only 45 variables were extracted from the MIMIC IV dataset, excluding Procalcitonin (PCT) due to its unavailability, with feature distributions detailed in eTable 5.

sec.title: Development of time-Varying ML models for predicting hemodynamic instability
sec.p:
We developed a series of time-varying predictive models, each of them utilizing 46 features from hours before intervention (Fig. 2, eFig. 5a, eFig. 5b). The eXtreme Gradient Boosted Ensembles of Decision Trees (XGBoost) classifier (eFig. 5b) was finally selected for each predictive model per hour, after employing a series of binary classifiers [11]. Data of VGHTPE 2010 cohort were divided into training, validation, and testing sets at a 2:2:1 ratio following 5-fold cross-validation scheme to prevent overfitting. Notably, the data used for training, validation, and testing were completely distinct, with no overlap between the sets. Up sampling of positive cases with stratification were used to ensure an even class distribution. Bayesian-searched hyperparameters were used for fine-tuning. The full process adhered to the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) + AI Checklist [12]. For each prediction model, we initially set the threshold as 0.5 for event firing. Fig. 2
a. Data on patient admissions was extracted from the Philips ICCA, adhering to specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. Before serving as input for the model, values considered clinically implausible, errors specific to variables, and other artifacts underwent automatic exclusion through the application of variable-specific algorithms. 24 predictive models encompassing 24 hours leading to hemodynamic intervention were then developed to establish a time-varying alarm system effectively. These models were trained on the extracted labels and features. The chosen classifier for the model was the extreme gradient-boosted ensembles of decision trees (XGBoost). b. Ensemble way for each of 24 models with imbalanced data. c. The proposed early warning system for hemodynamic instability comprises a 2nd alarm rule, i.e. alarm rate in 24 predicting models. The example is an optimal alarm policy on the balance of precision and recall, which has 65% of 24 predicted outputs surpassing 0.5. Precision is the proportion of alarms correctly predicting events, and recall is defined as the fraction of any alarm that correctly predicts events over the total number of true alarms within the preceding 24 hours. The system can lead 7 hours before the onset of hemodynamic interventions

sec.title: Development of Time-varying Hemodynamic Early Warning Score (TvHEWS)
sec.p: We set an alpha value as an additional rule to optimize the alarm policy for the proposed early warning system based on 24 time-varying models. The alpha value was set as an alarm rate in 24 predicting models, i.e. percentage of predicted value over the firing threshold. Precision of this system was calculated as the proportion of correct predictions above the alpha value, whereas recall was the proportion of correct predictions relative to the total number of true alarms. In this system, the alpha value was optimized to balance precision and recall across different cohorts, as illustrated in Fig. 2c. Adjustments to the alpha value were made across different cohorts to enhance the performance of the TvHEWS system (more detailed information is provided in Supplement Pages 35–36).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Nonparametric tests were applied since the population data did not have a normal distribution [13]. The Kruskal-Wallis test was used to test the significance of continuous variables in the form of medians and quartiles across both groups. Fisher’s exact test was used to test the categorical variables. All tests were conducted via a two-sided approach, and a P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), the area under the precision‒recall curve (AUPRC), precision, recall, and specificity of the model were used to evaluate the performance of this early warning system in all internal, prospective, and external cohorts. False and missing alarm rates were also assessed to evaluate their potential for application in clinical practice.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and prevalence of hemodynamic instability
sec.p: We used three patient cohort datasets for training and validation of the early warning system: VGHTPE 2010 for training and internal validation, VGHTPE 2022 for forward retrospective validation at the same site, and MIMIC IV for retrospective external validation. Among the 19,594 ICU stays in the final VGHTPE 2010 cohort, 18,438 patients aged ≥ 20 years were identified following both the inclusion and exclusion criteria shown in Fig. 1. A total of 19.9% (3,671) of the patients were in the unstable group. The remaining 80.1% (14,767) of patients were in the stable group. Table 1 shows that patients in the unstable group had significantly higher acute physiology and chronic health evaluation II (APACHE II) scores in the first six hours admitted to the ICU (24.8 vs. 19.0, p < 0.001), higher mortality rates (43.3% vs. 14.3%, p < 0.001), and longer ICU stay hours (288 h vs. 114 h, p < 0.001). Compared with stable patients, unstable patients were admitted less often from the emergency department (44.8% vs. 47.3%, p < 0.001), and no significant differences were found in age (p = 0.064) or gender (p = 0.553) between the unstable and stable groups. Using the same inclusion and exclusion criteria, 150 out of 700 ICU patients (21.4%) in the VGHTPE 2022 cohort experienced hemodynamic instability, serving as a forward retrospective validation for the TvHEWS. For the external validation with the MIMIC IV, 5,475 out of 47,492 ICU patients (11.5%) met the same criteria and experienced hemodynamic instability. MIMIC IV patients in the unstable group presented a notably higher APACHE II score within the first 6 h of admission to the ICU (14.0 vs. 10.0, p < 0.001), a higher mortality rate (30.2% vs. 6.6%, p < 0.001), and an extended duration of ICU stay (165 h vs. 41 h, p < 0.001). Detailed characteristics can be found in eTable 6. Moreover, compared with the training cohort VGHTPE 2010, the overall MIMIC IV cohort had a lower APACHE II score (20.1 vs. 10.0), fewer ICU stay hours (136 h vs. 45 h), and a lower mortality rate (20.1% vs. 8.9%).

sec.title: Performance of time-varying ML models for predicting hemodynamic instability
sec.p: 24 time-varying predictive models were fit from 1 h to 24 h before hemodynamic intervention (eFig.5a). The models were developed via XGBoost, and they were implemented without any missing data imputation after data processing (eFig. 5a and 5b). The model at 1 h before hemodynamic intervention demonstrated an optimal AUROC (0.94) in VGHTPE 2010, with precision, and recall of 0.77, and 0.85 respectively with setting the threshold as 0.5 for event firing, shown in eTable 7. The AUROC was 0.91, accompanied by precision and recall values of 0.76 and 0.83, respectively, even for the model at 24 h before hemodynamic intervention, shown in eTable 7. The median AUROC across 24 models was calculated as 0.91 (95% CI: [0.91, 0.92]), with corresponding medians for precision and recall recorded at 0.76 (95% CI: [0.76, 0.77]) and 0.83 (95% CI: [0.83, 0.83]), respectively.

sec.title: Performance of Time-varying Hemodynamic Early Warning Score (TvHEWS)
sec.p: In the VGHTPE 2010 cohort, the optimal alpha value for the early warning system with 24 time-varying models was 65%, with a higher recall value (0.760) than precision (0.711), shown in eTable 8. The alarm policy was applied to internal, forward retrospective, and external testing cohorts. The AUROCs of TvHEWS in VGHTPE 2010, VGHTPE 2022, and MIMIC IV were 0.93, 0.92, and 0.82, respectively (Fig. 3a), and the AUPRC values were 0.82, 0.79, and 0.61, respectively (Fig. 3b). The false alarm rate (0.077, 0.058, 0.033) remained at the lower level, and the missed alarm rates were 0.24, 0.327, and 0.638 (eTable 8, eTable 9, eTable 10).

caption.p: Performance of TvHEWS (a) A receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) was created for predicting hemodynamic instability, incorporating the alarm policy. This facilitated a comparative analysis across the three cohort datasets. (b) A precision‒recall curve (PRC) was generated for predicting hemodynamic instability with the implemented alarm policy, facilitating a comparative analysis across the three cohort datasets

sec.p: In the VGHTPE 2022 cohort, the optimal alpha value was 60% of the predicted values > 0.5 (precision vs. recall: 0.753 vs. 0.733) or 55% of the predicted values > 0.5 (precision vs. recall: 0.740 vs. 0.760) (eTable 9). For the MIMIC IV cohort, the optimal alpha value was identified as the 35% predicted value > 0.5, resulting in a precision of 0.586 and a recall of 0.562. When the alpha value was set to 65% of the predicted values > 0.5, the precision and recall yielded values of 0.723 and 0.362, respectively (eTable 10).

sec.title: Evaluation of potential clinical benefit and lead time before intervention
sec.p: By applying the VGHTPE 2010 alpha value to the other two cohorts, we were able to calibrate the alignment between the predicted and observed risk, resulting in Brier scores of 0.082 for VGHTPE 2010, 0.085 for VGHTPE 2022, and 0.116 for MIMIC IV (Fig. 4). Notably, the dark blue line within the calibration results for the VGHTPE 2010 cohort clearly manifests as alignment with the ideal calibration curve at both extremities. Extreme underestimation or overestimation of the risk point was also observed at approximately 0.4–0.6 in the VGHTPE 2022 cohort because of scattered data in this range of risk. Remarkably, although the optimal alpha value for MIMIC IV was 35% with a threshold value > 0.5, MIMIC IV essentially coincides with the ideal calibration curve by applying the optimal alpha value of 65% with the threshold value > 0.5 of VGHTPE2010.

caption.p: Calibration plots. The calibration plot, featuring VGHTPE 2010, VGHTPE 2022, and MIMIC IV, is a tool for assessing the agreement between predictions and observations

sec.p: We also investigated the lead time of TvHEWS under our time-varying alarm policy, i.e. setting the alpha value as 65% in these three cohorts. Figure 5 shows the distribution of the timing of the initial alarm within the 24 h preceding an event. Notably, 95% of unstable patients were identified with a lead time within 7 h prior to hemodynamic interventions in the VGHTPE 2010 cohort. For the VGHTPE 2022 cohort, a lead time of 8.6 h allows the identification of 95% of unstable patients before hemodynamic intervention, whereas in the MIMIC IV cohort, the lead time can occur 21 h in advance.

caption.p: Leading time plot. The temporal distribution of the alarm within 24 h preceding an event reveals that, for VGHTPE 2010, VGHTPE 2022, and MIMIC IV, 95% of unstable patients (in the red frame) were identified within a lead time of 7 h before hemodynamic intervention in the VGHTPE 2010 cohort. In the VGHTPE 2020 cohort, 95% of unstable patients were identified within a lead time of 8.6 h before hemodynamic intervention. In the MIMIC IV cohort, 95% of unstable patients were identified within a lead time of 21 h before hemodynamic intervention

sec.title: Model performance in different subgroups
sec.p: We also evaluated the system performance in both VGHTPE 2022 (eFig. 2a and b) and MIMIC IV cohorts (eFig. 2c and d) with varying admission sources. Using the TPEVGH 2010 alarm policy, the VGHTPE 2022 respiratory group achieved AUROCs and AUPRCs of 1.0. In the MIMIC IV respiratory group, the same policy resulted in an AUROC of 0.80 and an AUPRC of 0.65. For the cardiovascular group, the AUROCs were similar in the two cohorts (VGHTPE 2022: 0.89 vs. MIMIC IV: 0.83), and the AUPRCs were slightly different (VGHTPE 2022: 0.64 vs. MIMIC IV: 0.72). For the gastrointestinal tract, both AUROCs and AUPRCs performed better in VGHTPE 2022 (AUROCs: 0.94 vs. 0.84; AUPRCs: 0.80 vs. 0.68). For the trauma group, although VGHTPE 2022 had better AUROCs (0.93 vs. 0.84), the AUPRCs were close (0.63 vs. 0.64).

We also evaluated the system performance on different genders, APACHE II, admission type, surgical status and mortality groups in VGHTPE 2022 and MIMIC IV cohorts respectively (eFigs. 3 and 4). Surgical patients had higher precision and recall for cardiovascular patients in both the VGHTPE 2022 (eFig. 3a) and MIMIC IV groups (eFig. 4a). For gastrointestinal patients and another group, surgical patients had worse precision and recall in the VGHTPE 2022 cohort (eFig. 3a and 4a). Patients with lower APACHE II scores (0–15) in both the VGHTPE 2022 cohort and the MIMIC IV cohort demonstrated lower precision and recall (eFig. 3b. and eFig. 4b.). For the VGHTPE 2022 cohort, our model has better performance in males in terms of both precision and recall. Patients in the emergency group had lower recall and precision. Patients in the medical group also had better precision and recall than did those in the surgical group. The recall rate and precision rate were higher in the death group than in the surviving group (eFig 3c). For the MIMIC IV cohort, similar results were obtained for males and patients not from the emergency department in the VGHTPE 2022 cohort. However, the model performance was better for patients in the surgical group and the survival group (eFig. 4c).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In our study, we introduced a novel dynamic early warning system called TvHEWS. Traditional time window fixed prediction models often fail to adequately respond to the fluctuating conditions of critically ill ICU patients. We computed 24 models at one-hour intervals to address not only the representation of patients’ status at a fixed time window but also the fluctuation of patients’ status for 24 h. Using the alpha value of the training dataset, the AUROC was greater than 0.8 even in the external validation dataset and greater than 0.9 in the prospective validation dataset (AUROC of VGHTPE 2010 vs. VGHTPE 2022 vs. MIMIC IV: 0.93 vs. 0.92 vs. 0.82) without compromising the AUPRC (AUPRC of VGHTPE 2010 vs. VGHTPE 2022 vs. MIMIC IV: 0.82 vs. 0.79 vs. 0.61), whereas the AUROC decreased to less than 0.80 in an external cohort in the previous studies [6, 8]. External validation is critical to quantify the generalizability of a risk prediction model, whereas only 5–7.1% of published studies were externally validated [5, 9, 14].

In addition, as a continuous monitoring system, the higher false alarm rate is always an issue for further alarm fatigue [15–18]. TvHEWS demonstrated a lower false positive rate in all internal, prospective, and external validation cohorts (VGHTPE 2010: 0.077; VGHTPE 2022: 0.058; MIMIC IV: 0.033) while finding a balance between precision and recall. Considering that the false alarm rate remained at a lower level even in the MIMIC IV cohort, it provides one possibility for the model with generalization ability [19–21]. Notably, TvHEWS can identify 95% of patients at risk of hemodynamic instability at least 7 h in advance of clinical interventions. This substantial lead time is clinically significant in the ICU setting, where early recognition and proactive management of circulatory deterioration are critical. A 7-hour predictive window offers a valuable opportunity for clinicians to optimize fluid resuscitation strategies, titrate vasoactive medications, or initiate diagnostic evaluations before overt instability occurs—potentially reducing morbidity, preventing organ dysfunction, and improving patient outcomes.

Calibration plots also demonstrated that the TvHEWS under the alpha value in the VGHTPE 2010 cohort had aligned agreement between the predicted and observed values in all three cohorts (Brier scores: 0.082, 0.085, and 0.116 in the VGHTPE 2010, 2022 and MIMIC IV cohorts, respectively), although extreme underestimation or overestimation of the risk can be observed at approximately 0.4–0.6 due to scattered data in this range of the VGHTPE 2022 cohort. TvHEWS tends to overestimate the risk when the incidence of the validation cohort is lower than that of the training cohort since up sampling methods were used in constructing classifiers to learn comprehensive information [22–25].

However, performance drift was still observed between the training and external validation cohorts. From VGHTPE 2010 to MIMIC IV, after adjusting for incidence, the recall still decreased from 0.76 in the VGHTPE 2010 cohort to 0.36 in the MIMIC IV cohort, although the precision was still greater (0.71 vs. 0.73, respectively). The lower recall in MIMIC-IV likely reflects both case-mix difference and labeling disparities: First, MIMIC patients have lower severity.(APACHE II median 10 vs. 20.1 in VGHTPE). Second, different hemodynamic management practices may alter the intervention labeling. Third, PCT was missing in MIMIC-IV, reducing model informativeness. Despite the recall drop, the precision remained high (0.72) and AUROC still above 0.8, suggesting the model is still useful in screening high-risk patients even in a different healthcare setting. We emphasized the importance of site-specific threshold calibration and alpha value tuning in this context. To address this challenge, we recommend adjusting the alpha value for TvHEWS but not retraining the model while applying it in different clinical practices.

Based on our VGHTPE cohort, early identification by TvHEWS could potentially allow interventions up to 7 h earlier in 95% of unstable patients. Assuming a conservative 10% reduction in mortality based on literature linking timely intervention to improved survival, TvHEWS may contribute to preventing approximately 150–200 deaths annually in our ICU population.

External validation is suggested to evaluate the efficacy and generalizability of ML models. However, regarding the external validation of structural data in different cohorts, the performance always decreases for many reasons, including differences in feature distributions, case-mixed effects, and even disease incidence. The incidence of hemodynamic instability differs between VGHTPE 2010 and MIMIC IV. VGHTPE has a greater incidence of hemodynamic instability than MIMIC IV does (19.9% vs. 11.5%) (Table 1, eTable 6). In our study, compared with the VGHTPE 2010 dataset and the external validation dataset MIMIC IV, some features have different median values. The median BUN (blood urea nitrogen) and Cr (creatinine) levels in the VGHTPE 2010 and MIMIC IV groups were 31 mg/dl vs. 18 mg/dl and 1.5 mg/dl vs. 0.9 md/dl, respectively. These findings indicate that the VGHTPE 2010 cohort has worse renal function. The median FiO2 (inspired fraction of oxygen) and PaCO2 (partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the artery) in VGHTPE 2010 and MIMIC IV are 52.9% vs. 20% and 29.7 mmHg vs. 40 mmHg, respectively. The VGHTPE 2010 cohort has severe ventilation issues, with higher FiO2 and lower PaCO2. The blood sugar control also differed between the two cohorts. The median glucose value was 160.5 mg/dl in VGHTPE 2010 and 129 mg/dl in MIMIC IV. The recent recommended blood glucose control target in critically ill patients is 140 to 200 mg/dl [26]. The VGHTPE 2010 has a more liberal blood glucose control target. The SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score is related to disease severity. The median SOFA score was 8 in VGHTPE 2010 and 4 in MIMIC IV (eTable 11). The VGHTPE 2010 cohort has more severe disease conditions than the MIMIC IV cohort does.

Many different organ systems and complicated conditions can cause hemodynamic instability. The features that were selected in this study were selected not only based on data analysis but also on clinical considerations. The features selected in TvHEWS differ from those reported in previous studies. Cardiac output was excluded in the candidates since the missing ratio was > 60% of the cohort [7]. It is very practical and easy to use in the real clinical environment since each model in TvHEWS allows missing values as input. Therefore, although procalcitonin (PCT) is not available in the MIMIC IV, we set it all to null values as inputs to evaluate system performance, and the final AUROC is still over 0.8. We also introduced ventilator settings such as ventilation mode, mean airway pressure, FiO2, PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), Td (tidal volume), etc. These respiratory features could represent the respiratory condition, mainly if ARDS (acute respiratory distress syndrome) occurs. ARDS has always been an important cause of hemodynamic instability [27]. In addition, multiple organ failure is also closely related to patient severity and high risks for hemodynamic instability [28–30]. Thus, we also used features such as total bilirubin, AST, and ALT to evaluate liver function and BUN, Cr, and urine output to evaluate renal function. Hemograms and coagulation profiles are also a concern in our model because they are also related to unstable conditions in ICU patients.

TvHEWS still has several constraints for improvement. Enhancing predictive power involves integrating hemodynamic variables and considering factors such as sonography and antibiotics. Additionally, an area for improvement is the lack of prospective validation from other hospitals. Although the VGHTPE 2022 cohort from the same hospital demonstrated strong prospective validation results, this confirmed only the model’s performance at that specific site. Similarly, while the MIMIC cohort showed strong external validation, representing results for the US cohort, additional prospective validation from other hospitals is needed to further confirm the model’s robustness. Future steps include pursuing such validation to strengthen its clinical applicability.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: TvHEWS addresses the challenge of early detection of hemodynamic instability to adequately respond to the fluctuating conditions of critically ill ICU patients. We believe that TvHEWS, is a flexible framework for forecasting the conditions of critically ill patients, whose statuses are continuously changing over time. Further prospective validation in other hospitals is needed to confirm its robustness across diverse settings.
